97696899.title: Natural_Dis-tinction_Un-natural_Selection
97696899.extract:
**Natural Dis-tinction Un-natural Selection** is the thirty-third collection by British fashion designer Alexander McQueen, presented as his Spring/Summer 2009 runway show in Paris on October 3, 2008. The collection was widely recognized for its bold conceptual approach, innovative use of digital print technology, and compelling environmental themes, marking a significant moment in McQueen's career and in contemporary fashion history.


The overarching theme of Natural Dis-tinction Un-natural Selection explored the complex interplay between natural forms and artificial or industrial forces. McQueen drew inspiration from Charles Darwin's theories on evolution and the Industrial Revolution, questioning humanity's impact on the environment through dramatic juxtapositions of organic motifs and synthetic materials. The designer sought to interrogate the consequences of human intervention in nature, with recurring motifs of wildlife, minerals, and mechanical structures reflecting both fragility and resilience.

Central to the collection were engineered digital prints-crystal patterns, wood grains, flowers, and geometric mineral formations. These intricate designs were not only visually arresting but also conceptually charged, embodying the collection's focus on the collision between the biological and the manmade.


The presentation took place at Le 104, 5 Rue Curial, Paris, in an art space formerly used as a morgue, creating an atmosphere that reinforced the show's themes. The catwalk was lined with antique taxidermy-including an elephant, giraffe, tiger, zebra, and polar bear-evoking questions of mortality and the lasting marks of human presence on the animal kingdom. At the end of the slope stood a metal globe projecting images of a sun, moon, and rotating earth, symbolizing global interconnectedness and the weight of ecological change.

The collection itself was divided into two sequences. The first featured garments characterized by soft colors, natural fabrics, and digitally printed imagery of wood grain and meadow flowers, often engineered to accentuate garment silhouettes. Notable elements included dresses cut from single pieces of fabric, silk flowers trapped within tulle, and decorative touches like whitework embroidery and beetle-wing sequins contrasted with metallic buttercups coated in acid-yellow enamel.

The second sequence emphasized harder, angular forms inspired by crystals, minerals, and architectural motifs. Prints morphed from diamond patterns into skeletons; bell-jar-shaped dresses and bodysuits were encrusted with Swarovski crystals in jet, gold, and silver. Fabric choices shifted toward synthetic materials such as Lycra and bonded leather, underscoring the collection's contemplation of the destructive capacity of industrial progress.


A central highlight of the collection was the **Bell Jar dress**, distinguished by its rounded silhouette and sculpted skirt intended to echo the shape of a Victorian specimen jar-a visual nod to Charles Darwin's scientific collections. Crafted primarily from net densely appliquéd with Swarovski crystals, the garment was described as "more crystal than textile," dazzling the viewer with its sparkle and exemplifying McQueen's penchant for pushing material boundaries.

Other standout pieces included digitally printed dresses with engineered placements matching their fabric shapes, mini dresses adorned with metallic buttercups, and ensembles featuring beetle-wing sequins and acid-yellow enamels. The collection's craftsmanship combined traditional techniques-whitework embroidery, historical fabric manipulations-with technological innovations such as precision digital printing, reflecting McQueen's vision of future-facing yet historically rooted fashion.

Upon its debut, the collection received praise for its restrained yet powerful execution. Critics noted that despite McQueen's reputation for theatrical excess, the SS2009 show stood out for its unexpected restraint and intellectual rigor. WWD's review highlighted it as one of the season's most intriguing presentations, contrasting with a generally lackluster fashion week.

Sarah Mower of Vogue remarked on the "bright, multicolored allover prints, engineered to fit around jackets, leggings, and cocoon dresses" as emblematic of a London design trend, noting how these patterns transcended the Paris runway to influence broader fashion discourse. Antonio Berardi praised the menswear component for returning to a classic McQueen aesthetic-stripped back, bold, and modern-and for infusing fundamental menswear forms with McQueen's distinctive sensibility.

McQueen himself stated that he was "not aiming to preach," but the work resonated deeply as commentary on climate anxiety, humanity's relationship with nature, and the perils of unchecked industrialization. His belief that "we're in danger of killing the planet through greed" became a thread throughout the collection's narrative.

Natural Dis-tinction Un-natural Selection has become part of the permanent records of major fashion exhibitions. A tan leather shoe from the collection appeared in Alexander McQueen: Savage Beauty, an influential retrospective held at the Victoria & Albert Museum and later at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. The exhibition's catalog featured a wood-grain digital print from the collection as endpapers, further cementing its cultural significance.

The **Bell Jar dress** featured prominently in these retrospectives, exemplified by conservation work undertaken by the V&A to preserve its dazzling crystalline surface. The garment's association with Cate Blanchett at the Los Angeles premiere of *The Curious Case of Benjamin Button* introduced it to wider public consciousness and added layers of meaning regarding its status as both fashion object and cultural artifact.

Digital print innovation and the integration of technical design in ready-to-wear fashion were directly influenced by the collection, helping set new standards for creativity and production methods in high fashion. McQueen's ability to merge the historical with the futuristic established enduring trends in wearable art.

Natural Dis-tinction Un-natural Selection stands as a testament to Alexander McQueen's visionary approach to fashion as both artistic expression and critical social commentary. Through the manipulation of print technology, material experimentation, and a carefully curated environment, McQueen invited audiences to reflect on the tensions inherent in nature versus civilization, past versus present, and beauty versus destruction.

The collection remains a pivotal moment in fashion history, demonstrating how creativity can be harnessed to probe ethical, philosophical, and ecological questions while simultaneously advancing the technical and aesthetic boundaries of the industry. Its legacy continues to inspire designers, curators, and critics, affirming McQueen's enduring influence on fashion and culture.
